$comment: RIFTBORN element definitions and effectiveness matrix. First-pass tuning values.
dual_element_rule: Multiply the attacker's multiplier against each of the defender's elements. A Tide/Gale defender hit by Volt takes 2.0 x 2.0 = 4.0.

escort_ability_rules.$comment: Answers decision 1 in 09-risks-and-roadmap.md: 'Limited — one resident gives an active ability.' One escort, one charge per encounter, no autonomous action. The escort never attacks on its own; that is the line between a limited companion and a pet sim.

tide.name: Undertow
tide.blurb: A surge of cold that drags at it.

gale.name: Downdraught
gale.blurb: Shoves it back and spoils its lunge.

gloom.name: Shroud
gloom.blurb: You go unseen. Ambush is back on the table.

lumen.name: Kindle
lumen.blurb: Lights what hides — including a weak point that has none.

battle_rules.$comment: Turn-based battle. Your Sanctuary residents fight; weapons became the capture step. Damage reuses the element chart above, and the catch roll reuses the Restraint maths in ammo.json, so four phases of balance work carry over instead of being thrown away. hp_fraction_damage is the share of the DEFENDER's health a power-50 move takes at equal attack stats: damage is relative because health is not, and an absolute base made a mirror match 6 turns at stage 1 and 118 turns against Karrahk.
battle_rules.$cap_comment: A fight between comparable monsters cannot end in one hit. Four terms in the damage formula each reach about 2x — move power, the same-element bonus, the type chart, the attack ratio — and they multiply. Measured over 60 fair matchups (same stage, same size class, different element), 35% of fights ended inside two turns and the average was 3.3, which leaves no room for a status, a swap or anything else the battle offers. The cap is conditional on outclass_ratio rather than universal because a mismatch SHOULD end in one hit: at cap 0.20 fair fights run 6.1 turns, two-turn fights drop to 0%, mirror matches are untouched at 9.7, and Karrahk still one-shots a Glimmerfly.
battle_rules.$hold_comment: How much a speed penalty costs a monster its TURN, not just its place in the order. Speed was read in exactly one line of the engine — who acts first — and both sides act every turn regardless, so 'held', 'anchored', 'chilled' and 'sedated' were four status moves that did essentially nothing. A slowed monster now loses its turn with probability (1 - speed factor) * hold_scale: held is 40%, anchored 45%, sedated 25%, chilled 20%. That is the paralysis model, and it is what makes a status move worth the turn it costs.

ember.name: Cinderbrand
ember.blurb: Sets it alight. It keeps burning.

tide.name: Coldshock
tide.blurb: Cold enough to slow anything down.

gale.name: Razorwind
gale.blurb: A thousand small cuts that do not close.

volt.blurb: One good jolt through the nervous system.

gloom.blurb: It gets heavy, and then it gets slow.

rift.blurb: Lets a little of the rift through. It hurts, and it helps.

universal_moves.name: Strike
universal_moves.$comment: Every monster knows it. Untyped, so it is never resisted and never boosted — and it has no PP, so it is what you are left with when everything else is spent. That is the whole point of it.

warden_moves.name: Covering Fire
warden_moves.$comment: Before you have a monster, you fight with the gun. It is deliberately weaker than a monster's move: the game wants you to catch something.

apex_phase_rules.$comment: Apex phases, shared by both combat modes. A phase is an HP band: phase = 1 + floor((1 - hp/maxHp) * phases), which is what the real-time arena already did. The point of a phase, in the bestiary's words, is that a long fight should be a sequence of different problems rather than the same shot repeated — so each one changes what the apex does, what it is wearing, and whether it can be taken at all.
apex_phase_rules.$transition_comment: The arena gives the apex 1.2 seconds of invulnerability while it re-forms, and wipes the Restraint you had built. The turn-based reading of that is: the turn a band breaks, the apex takes no further damage and does not act, and every status on it is shrugged off. Both rules exist to stop a burst carrying you through two phases at once, which is the one thing that would make phases decorative.
apex_phase_rules.$band_comment: A break advances ONE phase, even if the hit crossed two health bands. Measured before this rule, a Verdant party took Karrahk from phase 1 to phase 3 in a single hit and the whole of phase 2 never happened — the phases were a caption on a health bar. Guaranteeing one band per turn makes them content rather than probability.
apex_phase_rules.$damage_comment: The share of an apex's health any single move may take. Relative damage means the type chart multiplies a FRACTION of health, so a quadruple weakness with same-element bonus came to 0.9 of the bar in one hit while a resisted move came to 0.03 — measured, 4 hits to kill Karrahk with the right element against 38 with the wrong one. Both ends ruin a designed fight: one skips the phases, the other is a slog. The band keeps the chart pointing the right way (about 2.4x for bringing the counter) without letting it decide whether the fight happens at all. It applies to apexes only — Karrahk one-shotting a Glimmerfly is correct and stays.
apex_phase_rules.$catch_comment: An apex's capture chance is DESIGNED per phase rather than derived. The Restraint maths is built for a monster you could plausibly carry home; a Titan with 1100 base Restraint is not that, and the derived chance against Karrahk is 0.04% — indistinguishable from the 2% floor, so every phase read the same and the phase gate did nothing. catch_chance below is the chance at the ideal moment: badly wounded, sedated, heavy dart. The actual roll scales down from there by the ratio of your Restraint value to that ideal, so softening and sedating still matter and no new constants are invented.

apex_phases.$comment: One entry per phase, in order. weak_points and armour_scale are read by the real-time arena too, so the two modes cannot drift apart. catch_scale, moves, flat_effectiveness and conceal are the turn-based battle's.

karrahk.label: Sunken Plating
karrahk.blurb: Karrahk surfaces still sheathed in plating. Nothing you fire is reaching anything that matters.

karrahk.label: Floodtide
karrahk.blurb: The plating splits and the water comes with it. The ground is gone — everything is slower now.

karrahk.label: Spire Core
karrahk.blurb: The spire cracks open and the core is finally in the light. This is the window.

nyxhollow.label: Shroud
nyxhollow.blurb: Nyxhollow puts the light out. You can hear where it is and that is all.

nyxhollow.label: Hollow Eye
nyxhollow.blurb: The shroud tears and the eye opens. It can see you, and you can finally see it.

aeonrend_apex.label: First Seam
aeonrend_apex.blurb: A seam opens. Whatever you brought, it does not care — nothing is strong or weak against this.

aeonrend_apex.label: Second Seam
aeonrend_apex.blurb: The seam moves. Wherever you were aiming, it is not there any more.

aeonrend_apex.label: Third Seam
aeonrend_apex.blurb: Three seams now, and it is bleeding something that is not blood.

aeonrend_apex.label: Aeon
aeonrend_apex.blurb: It stops pretending to have a shape. This is the last of it, one way or the other.

$moves_comment: Four moves each: a quick one, a heavy one, something that is not damage, and Strike. PP is PER BATTLE and deliberately tight — three heavies in a fight that now runs six turns — so the menu is a sequencing decision rather than a button you hold. Before this, every element had exactly two damage moves and 'pick the biggest number' matched a type-chart-aware policy on 83% of turns.
